transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump has been talked out of livestreaming the Fort Hood shooter's execution in part
because it might fuel violent extremism.
NPR's Quill Lawrence reports Nidal Hassan will still face a firing squad this December.
The president was persuaded that it was against American values to livestream an execution
according to a U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution.
The official said Trump was also told the video might be used to recruit violent anti-U.S.
extremists, even putting U.S. troops deployed to the Middle East at risk.
Nidal killed 13 fellow soldiers, including a pregnant woman, on Fort Hood in 2009.
He was wounded in the aftermath and now uses a wheelchair.
A separate U.S. official on Capitol Hill, who was not authorized to speak publicly,
told NPR that it was Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth who called for the firing squad to
be televised, quote, "catching everyone by surprise."
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
Ukraine's resumed its attacks on Russia's oil refineries over President Trump's objections.
President Vladimir Zelensky tells The Financial Times he held off briefly, but not anymore.
That's one sign of division between Zelensky and Trump.
NPR's Greg Myry reports another, involves a disruption to the satellite communication
system on which Ukraine's war effort relies.
Ukraine's defense ministry is saying that this satellite network is back and working
as normal.
And by way of explanation, many people know the satellite communication system Starlink.
This is part of Elon Musk's empire.
But there's also a military version called Star Shield that he built for the U.S. government
and military.
The Pentagon shares this with Ukraine, which uses it to guide its drones.
But yesterday, Ukraine discovered quite abruptly that the Star Shield system had suddenly been
greatly restricted.
NPR's Greg Myry reporting, Medicare open enrollment begins today and runs through early
December.
NPR's Selena Simmons-Steffen reports those enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans or prescription
drug plans can check to make sure their plan still fits their needs.
This year, several million seniors will not be able to renew the same plan, as some insurance
companies have scaled back their Medicare options, even so.
Most beneficiaries are still facing quite a complex choice.
Jeannie Fugleston-Bennick studies Medicare at KFF, a nonpartisan health research organization.
It is probably pretty challenging to compare all of the options for the average person.
There are online tools to compare plans at Medicare.gov, and there are state health insurance
assistance programs, or SHPs, in every state staffed by experts who can walk people through
their options and help them enroll.
Selena Simmons-Steffen, NPR News.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle made their first joint public appearance today since
returning to the UK.
They visited several charities and greeted fans along the way.
It's NPR News.
The U.S. economy remains resilient, but consumers are feeling the pressure of higher prices
and higher borrowing costs.
New government figures show retail sales rose 0.8 percent in September.
That month, companies paid more for products and supplies before those items got to customers.
Wholesale prices were more than 6 percent higher than a year ago.
And the mortgage buyer Freddie Mac says there's still no change in the fixed rate for 30-year
loans.
The average is 7.4 percent.
The average rate on a 15-year loan popular for refinancing ticked down slightly this
week to 6.71 percent.
The world's leading manufacturers of cutting-edge microchips, and the machines that make them,
say business is robust.
Quarterly results from Taiwan's TSMC and the Dutch company ASML show no signs of the AI
boom ending any time soon.
Here's NPR's John Ruich.
Taiwan's TSMC says its profits surged 69 percent in the latest quarter, the sixth quarter in
a row of record earnings.
The company is the world's biggest contract chip maker, and its fate hinges increasingly
on demand from companies buying chips for AI data centers.
It says that demand is very strong and increasing.
Meanwhile, the Dutch company ASML, which makes the complex printing tools that fabricate
cutting-edge chips, also reported strong earnings this week.
It says demand for its chip-making machines is increasing, and it's trying to boost capacity
to meet it.
Despite all that, investors remain on edge about the flood of money going into AI, and
chip stocks have dipped in recent days.
John Ruich, NPR News.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Trump reportedly talked out of livestreaming Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's execution
Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries over Trump's objections, Zelensky tells FT
Ukraine's Starlink-based military satellite system, Star Shield, abruptly restricted then restored
Medicare open enrollment begins, with several million seniors facing plan changes
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle make first joint public appearance since returning to UK
US retail sales rise 0.8 percent in September as wholesale prices climb over 6 percent
Freddie Mac reports 30-year mortgage rate unchanged at 7.4 percent
TSMC and ASML report strong quarterly earnings amid continued AI chip demand
